graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Your working directory is empty, so there's no existing setup to build on. Here's what I recommend.

## Recommendation: a scheduled GitHub Actions check

For five side projects, a small repo with a scheduled workflow costs nothing, needs no server to maintain, and is easy to extend:

- **`sites.yml`**: lists your five URLs, the HTTP status you expect (and optionally a keyword that should appear on the page), and a timeout.
- **`.github/workflows/uptime.yml`**: runs every 5 minutes, sends a request to each URL, and fails if any check misses.
- **Alerts:** only when a site's state changes (up→down or down→up), so you don't get a message every 5 minutes during an outage. It can send to a free ntfy.sh topic (push notifications to your phone), a Discord or Slack webhook, or email.
- **Optional:** a status page on GitHub Pages built from the check history.

Caveats: GitHub's cron can run a few minutes late, and GitHub disables scheduled workflows after 60 days with no repo activity. The workflow can make a small commit to keep itself active, which also gives you an uptime history.

**If you'd rather not build anything:** UptimeRobot's free tier (50 monitors, 5-minute checks) or Better Stack's free tier (10 monitors) will cover five sites in about 10 minutes of setup, with a status page included. If all you want is alerts and you don't care about owning the setup, that's the faster route.

## To scaffold it, I need:
1. **The 5 URLs.** Health-check endpoints like `/health` are better than homepages if your projects have them.
2. **Where alerts should go:** ntfy, Discord, Slack, or email.
3. **Whether you want a public status page.**

Send those and I'll create the repo files here. I won't push anything or create GitHub repos without checking with you first.

cases.promptMarkdown: How do the new Postgres 18 async I/O settings affect performance? I'll want to come back to this later.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer explains io_method (worker default, io_uring Linux-only, sync), io_workers 3, effective_io_concurrency 16, and the benchmark finding (2-3x faster sequential scans on cloud disks with io_uring, little gain on local NVMe), and points to the saved vault page.
FAIL if facts are wrong or it does not mention saving the research.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Postgres 18 adds asynchronous I/O for reads, meaning it can request several blocks at once instead of waiting on each one. How much that helps depends mostly on how slow your storage is.

**Settings** (from the official docs)
- `io_method`: `worker` is the default and uses background I/O worker processes. `io_uring` is Linux-only and uses the kernel's async interface. `sync` gives you the pre-18 behaviour.
- `io_workers`: defaults to 3 and only matters when `io_method=worker`.
- `effective_io_concurrency`: the default is now 16, so more read-ahead is allowed out of the box.

**Performance** (from pganalyze's benchmarks, 2026-09-30)
- **Cloud or network disks:** sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`. Slow, high-latency storage gains the most because more requests can be waiting at the same time.
- **Local NVMe:** little gain.
- **`worker` vs `io_uring`:** the default `worker` mode gets most of the benefit, so you don't need `io_uring` to see a real improvement.

**What to do:** keep the default `worker` mode. Only try `io_uring` if you're on Linux, your storage is slow, and you benchmark it on your own workload first.

**What I couldn't confirm:** my sources were thin, just two short excerpts. They didn't say which operations beyond sequential scans use async I/O, whether writes are covered, when to raise `io_workers`, or whether changing `io_method` needs a restart. I've listed these as open questions on the page. One search result also gave the docs page a date of 2026-11-13, after today, so I saved that date as unknown.

I saved this to your research vault as **[[Postgres 18 async IO]]**, along with copies of both sources. It's listed in the index and research log, and the vault's check found no problems. I marked it to be re-checked within 90 days. Next time, you can ask me to look it up and fill in the open questions.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
I could only partly answer this. The feature question has an answer from one source, but I found nothing on bugs either way.

## What it supports

The only source I found is Valkey's own search topic page (https://valkey.io/topics/search/, dated 2026-10-01). It says Valkey 9 ships the search module as **valkey-search 1.2**, with:

- **Vector similarity search** using two index types: HNSW (approximate nearest neighbour) and FLAT (exact, brute-force).
- **Numeric and tag filters.**
- **Hybrid queries**, meaning a vector search combined with numeric or tag filters.
- **No full-text search yet.** The page says it's planned but not available.

In practice it's a vector database with metadata filtering, not a RediSearch replacement. If you need text queries like stemming, phrase matching or fuzzy search, it can't do them yet.

## Are people hitting bugs?

**I don't know.** Several searches aimed at GitHub, Reddit, Hacker News and Stack Overflow returned nothing relevant. I also tried to open the project's issue tracker directly and the fetch failed. So I have no evidence for or against bugs, and that doesn't mean there aren't any.

To check yourself, the best places are:

- **https://github.com/valkey-io/valkey-search/issues**: filter by the `bug` label, or search for `crash`, `cluster`, `replication`, `memory`.
- **The valkey-search release notes for 1.2.x**: point releases list fixed bugs, which shows where the rough edges have been.
- **Valkey's GitHub Discussions and Discord.**

If you tell me your use case (cluster mode, index size, whether you're replacing RediSearch), I can try more targeted searches.

cases.promptMarkdown: Is Drizzle ORM v1 production ready? I want to know what breaks before I upgrade.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer covers the v1 breaking changes (relational queries v2 default, drizzle-kit push renamed sync, driver versions), the open enum migration issue #5120 with its data-loss risk, the self-relation bug fixed in 1.0.3, separates what sources state from its own inference, and ends with a line listing the lanes or providers searched.
FAIL if it misses issue #5120, or has no coverage line, or mixes inference with cited fact without saying so.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer covers the v1 breaking changes (relational queries v2 default, drizzle-kit push renamed sync, driver versions), the open enum migration issue #5120 with its data-loss risk, the self-relation bug fixed in 1.0.3, separates what sources state from its own inference, and ends with a line listing the lanes or providers searched.
FAIL if it misses issue #5120, or has no coverage line, or mixes inference with cited fact without saying so.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Mostly yes. Drizzle ORM v1.0 has been stable since **2026-09-15** and early reports from production use are good. The big risk is **one open bug that can lose data** in generated migrations.

## What breaks when you upgrade (official upgrade guide)

1. **Relational queries v2 is now the default.** Any code using `db.query.*` (the `findMany`/`findFirst` style with `with:`) runs on the new engine. Expect to update your relation definitions, and check that results still come back in the shape you expect.
2. **`drizzle-kit push` is now `drizzle-kit sync`.** Update your package.json scripts, CI jobs and docs.
3. **Postgres drivers have minimum versions:** node-postgres (`pg`) 9+ or postgres.js 4+. Upgrade the driver first if you're on something older.

The guide I could pull listed only these three headline changes. Read the full migration guide on orm.drizzle.team before you start, because there may be smaller API changes it didn't show.

## Known v1 bugs to watch for

- **Issue #5120: enum changes drop and recreate the column.** It's still open (opened 2026-10-03, 61 comments). If you change a Postgres enum, the migration drizzle-kit generates can delete that column's data. The only workaround is to edit the generated SQL by hand before applying it. This is the main thing to worry about.
- **Issue #5188: relational queries v2 returned wrongly nested results for tables that relate to themselves** (e.g. parent/child). Fixed in **1.0.3** (2026-10-29), so go straight to ≥1.0.3, not 1.0.0.

## Recommendation

It's fine to upgrade if you:
- pin to **≥1.0.3**
- review every generated migration before running it, especially anything touching enums, until #5120 is fixed
- test your `db.query` calls against real data, not just type checks

A team blog post about running v1 in production for a month said the same: "solid, but review every generated migration." It's on a domain I don't recognise, so treat it as one data point, not proof.

I didn't find Drizzle in any package.json in this directory. If your project is somewhere else, point me at it and I'll find the code affected by these changes.

graders.name: answer

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer reports what the official sources say about v5 changes and clearly states that practitioner or community sentiment could not be checked (the social lane or last30days is unavailable), instead of asserting what people regret.
FAIL if it presents community regrets as findings without community sources.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
I couldn't find any first-hand accounts of people regretting the move to Tailwind v5. Two web searches turned up only the official announcement. No blog posts, Reddit or Hacker News threads, or GitHub issues about migration pain came back. v5 came out on 2026-08-20, less than three months ago, which may be why.

**What the announcement says changed** ([tailwindcss.com/blog/tailwindcss-v5](https://tailwindcss.com/blog/tailwindcss-v5)):
- CSS-first configuration is now the default, and the JavaScript config file (`tailwind.config.js`) has been **removed**.
- New defaults for container queries.
- It now uses the Lightning CSS engine.
- There's an upgrade tool: `npx @tailwindcss/upgrade@5`.

**Where problems are likely, based on those changes (this is my guess, not reported experience):**
- **Losing the JS config** is the most likely source of pain. Setups that build the theme with code (loops, computed values, settings shared with other tools, design tokens imported from JS) don't map neatly to static CSS config.
- **Plugins and presets** that relied on the JS config API may break or need updating, especially third-party ones that haven't released v5-compatible versions yet.
- **Changed container query defaults** could quietly shift layouts without causing any build errors. You'd have to check visually to catch it.
- **Lightning CSS** may handle edge cases differently from the old pipeline, for example custom PostCSS plugins in your chain or certain syntax and browser targets.

If you're deciding whether to upgrade a specific project, I can look through its Tailwind config and plugins and tell you which of these risks apply. I can also search more specific places, like GitHub issues on the tailwindcss repo or r/tailwindcss, for real reports.

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if the answer says the earlier vault page (Bun 1.1) was out of date, reports Bun 1.4 changes (node:cluster supported, about 99% of Node tests), and warns about the open keep-alive memory issue (#31877, fix targeted for 1.4.2).
FAIL if it repeats the old 1.1 verdict, or omits the open memory issue.

config.criteria:
PASS if the answer says the earlier vault page (Bun 1.1) was out of date, reports Bun 1.4 changes (node:cluster supported, about 99% of Node tests), and warns about the open keep-alive memory issue (#31877, fix targeted for 1.4.2).
FAIL if it repeats the old 1.1 verdict, or omits the open memory issue.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Short answer: almost, but not yet for production.** Bun 1.4 fixed most of the old compatibility gaps. There's one open memory bug that hits API servers directly, so I'd wait for 1.4.2.

**What's changed lately**
- **Bun 1.4 (released 2 Oct 2026)** ([blog](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4)):
  - `node:cluster` is now supported, and `worker_threads` is complete. These were long-standing blockers for multi-core servers.
  - It passes 99.1% of Node's own test suite.
  - It adds a built-in Postgres connection pool.
  - **Breaking change:** `Bun.serve()`'s default idle timeout went from 10s to 30s. If your load balancer has its own idle timeout, check that the two still line up.
- **Open blocker: [oven-sh/bun#31877](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/31877) (opened 20 Oct).** Memory keeps growing under sustained HTTP keep-alive load in 1.4.0. The maintainers have reproduced it and are aiming to fix it in 1.4.2, but the issue is still open. That's exactly the traffic pattern an API server sees behind a load balancer.
- **Real-world reports:** In an [r/node thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/node/comments/bun14) (12 Oct), one team moved an Express API to Bun 1.4 and saw p95 latency drop about 30%. Someone else in the same thread ran into the memory leak. That's one anecdote each way, not a benchmark.
- **Node side:** Node 24 is the Active LTS line (v24.11.0 came out 28 Oct), so staying on Node is a low-risk option.

**What I'd do**
1. Wait for 1.4.2 and confirm #31877 is closed.
2. Then run your actual server on Bun in staging, under sustained keep-alive load for a few hours, and watch memory.
3. Check your native addons and any less common `node:` APIs. The remaining 0.9% of failing tests is where surprises would come from.
4. Move one instance or a slice of traffic over before switching everything.

I couldn't check your server itself because there's no `package.json` under the current directory. If you point me at the repo, I can go through its dependencies and look for things likely to break on Bun.
